The saturated spectral radius for complete graphs

Zhengbo Chen Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, MOE-LSC, SHL-MAC, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200240, China
czb911@sjtu.edu.cn; xiaodong@sjtu.edu.cn    Xiao-Dong Zhang ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, MOE-LSC, SHL-MAC, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200240, China
czb911@sjtu.edu.cn; xiaodong@sjtu.edu.cn
Abstract

A graph is Kr+1K_{r+1}-saturated if it is Kr+1K_{r+1}-free and adding any missing edge creates a copy of Kr+1K_{r+1}. Kim, Kim, Kostochka, and O conjectured that Kr−1∨(n−r+1)​K1K_{r-1}\vee(n-r+1)K_{1} minimizes the spectral radius among all nn-vertex Kr+1K_{r+1}-saturated graphs. They proved the case r=2r=2, and the cases r=3r=3 and r∈{4,5}r\in\{4,5\} were subsequently established by Kim, Kostochka, O, Shi, and Wang, and by Wang and Hou, respectively. We settle the conjecture for all r≥3r\geq 3: if n≥r+1n\geq r+1 and GG is an nn-vertex Kr+1K_{r+1}-saturated graph, then

ρ⁡(G)≥r−2+(r−2)2+4​(r−1)​(n−r+1)2,\rho(G)\geq\frac{r-2+\sqrt{(r-2)^{2}+4(r-1)(n-r+1)}}{2},

with equality if and only if G≅Kr−1∨(n−r+1)​K1G\cong K_{r-1}\vee(n-r+1)K_{1}. We also prove O’s local two-walk conjecture for every r≥2r\geq 2:

∑w∈NG​(v)dG​(w)≥(r−2)​dG​(v)+(r−1)​(n−r+1)(v∈V⁡(G)).\sum_{w\in N_{G}(v)}d_{G}(w)\geq(r-2)d_{G}(v)+(r-1)(n-r+1)\qquad(v\in V(G)).

If GG has no universal vertex, the inequality holds with the additional term (r−1)​(r−2)(r-1)(r-2) on the right-hand side. This constant is best possible uniformly in nn for every fixed rr, and gives a strict improvement when r≥3r\geq 3. A corresponding spectral bound follows.

Keywords: Graph saturation; spectral radius; two-walk counts; α\alpha-critical graphs.
AMS Classification: 05C50; 05C35; 05C07

1 Introduction

For a fixed graph FF, a graph GG is called FF-saturated if GG is FF-free and G+eG+e contains a copy of FF for every e∈E⁡(G¯)e\in E(\overline{G}). The saturation number sat⁡(n,F)\operatorname{sat}(n,F) is the minimum number of edges in an nn-vertex FF-saturated graph.

A spectral analogue is obtained by minimizing the adjacency spectral radius. Writing ρ⁡(G)\rho(G) for the adjacency spectral radius of GG, we define the spectral saturation number by

satρ(n,F)=min{ρ(G):|V(G)|=n,G is F-saturated}.\operatorname{sat}_{\rho}(n,F)=\min\bigl\{\rho(G):|V(G)|=n,\ G\text{ is }F\text{-saturated}\bigr\}.

The associated extremal problems are to determine these two parameters and characterize the graphs attaining the respective minima. In this paper, we focus on the spectral saturation problem for complete graphs.

For integers r≥2r\geq 2 and n≥r+1n\geq r+1, let Sn,r=Kr−1∨(n−r+1)​K1S_{n,r}=K_{r-1}\vee(n-r+1)K_{1}. The theorem of Erdős, Hajnal, and Moon [2] states that every nn-vertex Kr+1K_{r+1}-saturated graph GG satisfies

e⁡(G)≥(r−1)​n−(r2),e(G)\geq(r-1)n-\binom{r}{2},

with equality if and only if G≅Sn,rG\cong S_{n,r}. Thus the minimum edge count and its unique extremal structure are completely determined.

A natural spectral analogue asks whether Sn,rS_{n,r} also minimizes the adjacency spectral radius among graphs in the same class. This replaces the number of edges by a quantity that also reflects how those edges are distributed among the vertices. Its spectral radius is

ρ⁡(Sn,r)=r−2+(r−2)2+4​(r−1)​(n−r+1)2.\rho(S_{n,r})=\frac{r-2+\sqrt{(r-2)^{2}+4(r-1)(n-r+1)}}{2}.

The classical edge bound alone does not yield this spectral bound: combining it with ρ⁡(G)≥2​e​(G)/n\rho(G)\geq 2e(G)/n gives only

ρ⁡(G)≥2​(r−1)−r⁡(r−1)n,\rho(G)\geq 2(r-1)-\frac{r(r-1)}{n},

which remains bounded for fixed rr, whereas ρ⁡(Sn,r)∼(r−1)​n\rho(S_{n,r})\sim\sqrt{(r-1)n} as n→∞n\to\infty. Obtaining the sharp spectral bound therefore requires additional information about the local structure imposed by saturation. Kim, Kim, Kostochka, and O [4] proposed the following conjecture.

Conjecture 1.1.

Let r≥3r\geq 3 and n≥r+1n\geq r+1. If GG is an nn-vertex Kr+1K_{r+1}-saturated graph, then ρ⁡(G)≥ρ⁡(Sn,r)\rho(G)\geq\rho(S_{n,r}).

Kim, Kim, Kostochka, and O [4] first obtained an asymptotically sharp lower bound for general rr. More precisely, by establishing a sharp lower bound on ∑v∈V⁡(G)dG​(v)2\sum_{v\in V(G)}d_{G}(v)^{2}, they proved that every nn-vertex Kr+1K_{r+1}-saturated graph GG, with n≥r+1n\geq r+1 and r≥2r\geq 2, satisfies

ρ⁡(G)≥(r−1)​(n−1)2+(r−1)2​(n−r+1)n.\rho(G)\geq\sqrt{\frac{(r-1)(n-1)^{2}+(r-1)^{2}(n-r+1)}{n}}.

For every fixed rr, this bound is asymptotically sharp as n→∞n\to\infty. They also settled the case r=2r=2: every nn-vertex K3K_{3}-saturated graph satisfies ρ⁡(G)≥n−1\rho(G)\geq\sqrt{n-1}, with equality if and only if GG is the star K1,n−1K_{1,n-1} or a Moore graph of diameter two.

Further progress established the conjectured exact bound for several small values of rr. Kim, Kostochka, O, Shi, and Wang [5] proved Conjecture 1.1 for r=3r=3 and showed that K2∨(n−2)​K1K_{2}\vee(n-2)K_{1} is the unique extremal graph. Wang and Hou [9] subsequently confirmed the conjecture for r=4r=4 and r=5r=5. Ai, Liu, O, and Zhang [1] independently established the case r=4r=4 by proving that every nn-vertex K5K_{5}-saturated graph GG satisfies

∑w∈NG​(v)dG​(w)≥2​dG​(v)+3​(n−3)for every ​v∈V⁡(G).\sum_{w\in N_{G}(v)}d_{G}(w)\geq 2d_{G}(v)+3(n-3)\qquad\text{for every }v\in V(G).

Their result provides another proof of the sharp spectral bound for K5K_{5}-saturated graphs, including the uniqueness of the extremal graph K3∨(n−3)​K1K_{3}\vee(n-3)K_{1}.

Local walk counts provide a way to capture the additional structural information needed for the spectral problem. If A=A⁡(G)A=A(G) is the adjacency matrix and 𝟏\mathbf{1} is the all-ones vector, then (A​𝟏)v=dG​(v)(A\mathbf{1})_{v}=d_{G}(v) and

(A2​𝟏)v=∑w∈NG​(v)dG​(w),(A^{2}\mathbf{1})_{v}=\sum_{w\in N_{G}(v)}d_{G}(w),

the number of walks of length two starting at vv. A pointwise comparison between these quantities can be converted into a quadratic inequality for the spectral radius by weighting with a positive Perron eigenvector. Such a comparison also retains information at individual vertices, which is useful for determining the equality case. This motivates the following local two-walk conjecture, recorded in [8, Problem 13B-2].

Conjecture 1.2.

Let r≥2r\geq 2 and n≥r+1n\geq r+1. If GG is an nn-vertex Kr+1K_{r+1}-saturated graph, then every v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) satisfies

∑w∈NG​(v)dG​(w)≥(r−2)​dG​(v)+(r−1)​(n−r+1).\sum_{w\in N_{G}(v)}d_{G}(w)\geq(r-2)d_{G}(v)+(r-1)(n-r+1).

Kim, Kostochka, O, Shi, and Wang [5, Theorem 2.2] proved that Conjecture 1.2 implies the spectral bound in Conjecture 1.1. We establish the local conjecture for every r≥2r\geq 2 and determine the spectral equality case for every r≥3r\geq 3. Consequently, for r≥3r\geq 3, the graph Sn,rS_{n,r} uniquely minimizes both the number of edges and the adjacency spectral radius among nn-vertex Kr+1K_{r+1}-saturated graphs. This gives an exact spectral counterpart to the classical Erdős–Hajnal–Moon theorem. For r≥3r\geq 3, we also obtain a sharp improvement of the local inequality for graphs with no universal vertex, together with a corresponding stronger spectral bound.

Theorem 1.3.

Let r≥3r\geq 3 and n≥r+1n\geq r+1. If GG is an nn-vertex Kr+1K_{r+1}-saturated graph, then

ρ⁡(G)≥r−2+(r−2)2+4​(r−1)​(n−r+1)2,\rho(G)\geq\frac{r-2+\sqrt{(r-2)^{2}+4(r-1)(n-r+1)}}{2},

with equality if and only if G≅Kr−1∨(n−r+1)​K1G\cong K_{r-1}\vee(n-r+1)K_{1}.

Theorem 1.4.

Let r≥2r\geq 2 and n≥r+1n\geq r+1. If GG is an nn-vertex Kr+1K_{r+1}-saturated graph, then every v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) satisfies

∑w∈NG​(v)dG​(w)≥(r−2)​dG​(v)+(r−1)​(n−r+1).\sum_{w\in N_{G}(v)}d_{G}(w)\geq(r-2)d_{G}(v)+(r-1)(n-r+1). (1.1)

If GG has no universal vertex, then

∑w∈NG​(v)dG​(w)≥(r−2)​dG​(v)+(r−1)​(n−1)\sum_{w\in N_{G}(v)}d_{G}(w)\geq(r-2)d_{G}(v)+(r-1)(n-1) (1.2)

holds. For r≥3r\geq 3, this improves the right-hand side of (1.1) by (r−1)​(r−2)(r-1)(r-2); for r=2r=2, the two bounds coincide. The additional constant (r−1)​(r−2)(r-1)(r-2) is best possible uniformly in nn for every fixed rr.

The bound (1.2) also yields the following spectral consequence.

Corollary 1.5.

Let r≥2r\geq 2 and n≥r+1n\geq r+1. If GG is an nn-vertex Kr+1K_{r+1}-saturated graph with no universal vertex, then

ρ⁡(G)≥r−2+(r−2)2+4​(r−1)​(n−1)2.\rho(G)\geq\frac{r-2+\sqrt{(r-2)^{2}+4(r-1)(n-1)}}{2}. (1.3)

For every r≥2r\geq 2, equality is attained by G=C2​r+1¯G=\overline{C_{2r+1}}.

Our main new ingredient is a uniform bound on independent set multiplicities. For comparison, the proof for K5K_{5}-saturated graphs in [1, Section 4, Case 2] estimates the local two-walk count through a case analysis involving triangles in a vertex neighborhood. In Proposition 3.1, we work in the complement and control the overlaps of independent sets using two inequalities. Hajnal’s intersection–union lemma bounds the sum of the sizes of the union and intersection of a family of maximum independent sets. Surányi’s inequality bounds the neighborhood of that intersection inside an anti-neighborhood. Together, they yield the multiplicity estimate (3.1) for every r≥2r\geq 2.

Both ingredients apply without a connectedness hypothesis on the complement. The final reduction therefore consists of deleting the universal vertices, applying Proposition 3.1 to the remaining graph, and tracking the local surplus when the deleted vertices are restored.

2 Preliminaries

All graphs considered in this paper are finite and simple. For a graph GG, let V⁡(G)V(G) and E⁡(G)E(G) denote its vertex set and edge set, respectively, and write e⁡(G)=|E⁡(G)|e(G)=|E(G)|. For a vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), let NG​(v)N_{G}(v) denote its open neighborhood, let NG​[v]=NG​(v)∪{v}N_{G}[v]=N_{G}(v)\cup\{v\} denote its closed neighborhood, and write dG​(v)=|NG​(v)|d_{G}(v)=|N_{G}(v)| for its degree. A vertex of an nn-vertex graph is called universal if it has degree n−1n-1. Throughout the paper, we write H=G¯H=\overline{G} for the complement of GG.

For two vertex-disjoint graphs G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}, their join, denoted by G1∨G2G_{1}\vee G_{2}, is obtained from their disjoint union by adding all edges between V⁡(G1)V(G_{1}) and V⁡(G2)V(G_{2}). As usual, KrK_{r} denotes the complete graph on rr vertices, CℓC_{\ell} denotes the cycle on ℓ\ell vertices, and m​K1mK_{1} denotes the edgeless graph on mm vertices.

Given a graph FF, a graph GG is called FF-saturated if GG is FF-free but G+eG+e contains a copy of FF for every e∈E⁡(H)e\in E(H). Let A⁡(G)A(G) denote the adjacency matrix of GG, and let ρ⁡(G)\rho(G) denote its spectral radius. For v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), the number of walks of length two starting at vv is ∑w∈NG​(v)dG​(w)\sum_{w\in N_{G}(v)}d_{G}(w).

For A⊆V⁡(H)A\subseteq V(H), write NH​(A)=⋃a∈ANH​(a)N_{H}(A)=\bigcup_{a\in A}N_{H}(a) for its open neighborhood. An independent set has no internal edges, and α⁡(H)\alpha(H) denotes the maximum size of an independent set in HH. We call HH α\alpha-critical if α⁡(H−e)=α⁡(H)+1\alpha(H-e)=\alpha(H)+1 for every e∈E⁡(H)e\in E(H); isolated vertices are allowed in this definition.

For n≥r+1n\geq r+1, a graph GG is Kr+1K_{r+1}-saturated if and only if its complement H=G¯H=\overline{G} is α\alpha-critical and α⁡(H)=r\alpha(H)=r. Indeed, adding an missing edge of GG is deleting an edge of HH, and a new (r+1)(r+1)-clique is a new independent set of size r+1r+1 in HH.

Lemma 2.1 ([7, Theorem 3.5]).

Let HH be an α\alpha-critical graph without isolated vertices. Then, for every independent set A⊆V⁡(H)A\subseteq V(H) and every a∈Aa\in A,

dH​(a)≤|NH​(A)|−|A|+1.d_{H}(a)\leq|N_{H}(A)|-|A|+1. (2.1)
Lemma 2.2 ([3]).

Let GG be a graph and let H=G¯H=\overline{G}. If HH is α\alpha-critical without isolated vertices, then every a∈V⁡(H)a\in V(H) satisfies

dH​(a)≤|V⁡(H)|−2​α​(H)+1,dG​(a)≥2​α​(H)−2.d_{H}(a)\leq|V(H)|-2\alpha(H)+1,\qquad d_{G}(a)\geq 2\alpha(H)-2. (2.2)

The first inequality is Hajnal’s classical degree bound [3]; see also [7, Theorem 3.4].

Lemma 2.3.

Let HH be α\alpha-critical without isolated vertices, let z∈V⁡(H)z\in V(H), and let W=H⁡[V⁡(H)∖NH​[z]]W=H[V(H)\setminus N_{H}[z]]. Every independent set II of WW satisfies

|NW​(I)|≥|I|.|N_{W}(I)|\geq|I|.
Proof.

The set I∪{z}I\cup\{z\} is independent in HH. Moreover,

NH​(I∪{z})=NH​(z)​∪˙​NW​(I).N_{H}(I\cup\{z\})=N_{H}(z)\,\dot{\cup}\,N_{W}(I).

To check this identity, a neighbor of II outside NH​(z)N_{H}(z) is different from zz, since I⊆V⁡(W)I\subseteq V(W), and thus belongs to V⁡(W)V(W). Apply Lemma 2.1 to I∪{z}I\cup\{z\} at zz to obtain

dH​(z)≤dH​(z)+|NW​(I)|−|I|.d_{H}(z)\leq d_{H}(z)+|N_{W}(I)|-|I|.

Canceling dH​(z)d_{H}(z) proves the assertion. ∎

Lemma 2.4.

Let ℐ={I1,…,Is}\mathcal{I}=\{I_{1},\ldots,I_{s}\} be a family of maximum independent sets of a graph HH, where |Ii|=α⁡(H)|I_{i}|=\alpha(H). Then

|⋂i=1sIi|+|⋃i=1sIi|≥2​α​(H).\left|\bigcap_{i=1}^{s}I_{i}\right|+\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^{s}I_{i}\right|\geq 2\alpha(H).
Proof.

We proceed by induction on ss. The case s=1s=1 is immediate. Suppose s≥2s\geq 2. There are no edges between ⋂i=1s−1Ii\bigcap_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i} and ⋃i=1s−1Ii\bigcup_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i}: if c∈⋂i=1s−1Iic\in\bigcap_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i} and d∈⋃i=1s−1Iid\in\bigcup_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i}, then d∈Iid\in I_{i} for some i<si<s, while c∈Iic\in I_{i}. Hence

(Is∩⋃i=1s−1Ii)∪(⋂i=1s−1Ii)\left(I_{s}\cap\bigcup_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i}\right)\cup\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i}\right)

is independent, and therefore α⁡(H)≥|(Is∩⋃i=1s−1Ii)∪(⋂i=1s−1Ii)|=|Is∩⋃i=1s−1Ii|+|(⋂i=1s−1Ii)∖Is|\alpha(H)\geq\left|\left(I_{s}\cap\bigcup_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i}\right)\cup\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i}\right)\right|=\left|I_{s}\cap\bigcup_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i}\right|+\left|\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i}\right)\setminus I_{s}\right| =α⁡(H)−|Is∖⋃i=1s−1Ii|+|(⋂i=1s−1Ii)∖Is|,=\alpha(H)-\left|I_{s}\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i}\right|+\left|\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i}\right)\setminus I_{s}\right|,Which gives |Is∖⋃i=1s−1Ii|≥|(⋂i=1s−1Ii)∖Is|.\left|I_{s}\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i}\right|\geq\left|\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i}\right)\setminus I_{s}\right|. Thus the union gains at least as many vertices as the intersection loses when IsI_{s} is added.

By the induction hypothesis,

|⋂i=1sIi|+|⋃i=1sIi|≥|⋂i=1s−1Ii|+|⋃i=1s−1Ii|≥2​α​(H).\left|\bigcap_{i=1}^{s}I_{i}\right|+\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^{s}I_{i}\right|\geq\left|\bigcap_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i}\right|+\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^{s-1}I_{i}\right|\geq 2\alpha(H).

∎

3 Proofs of the main results

Proposition 3.1.

Let HH be an α\alpha-critical graph of order nn with no isolated vertices, and suppose that α⁡(H)=r≥2\alpha(H)=r\geq 2. Let G=H¯G=\overline{H}. Then every vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) satisfies

∑w∈NG​(v)dG​(w)≥(r−2)​dG​(v)+(r−1)​(n−1).\sum_{w\in N_{G}(v)}d_{G}(w)\geq(r-2)d_{G}(v)+(r-1)(n-1).
Proof.

Fix v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) and let

X=V⁡(H)∖NH​[v]=NG​(v),Y=NH​(v).X=V(H)\setminus N_{H}[v]=N_{G}(v),\qquad Y=N_{H}(v).

For each y∈Yy\in Y, choose and fix a set Iy⊆XI_{y}\subseteq X of size r−1r-1 such that {v,y}∪Iy\{v,y\}\cup I_{y} is independent in H−v​yH-vy.There may be more than one such set for a given yy; we choose one arbitrarily and keep this choice fixed throughout the proof. Such a choice is possible by the α\alpha-criticality of HH. In particular, IyI_{y} is independent in HH and Iy∩NH​(y)=∅I_{y}\cap N_{H}(y)=\varnothing. Moreover,

|Iy|=r−1,|{v}∪Iy|=r,|{v,y}∪Iy|=r+1.|I_{y}|=r-1,\qquad|\{v\}\cup I_{y}|=r,\qquad|\{v,y\}\cup I_{y}|=r+1.

Let

ℐ={Iy:y∈Y}\mathcal{I}=\{I_{y}:y\in Y\}

be the family of chosen sets. Distinct indices may correspond to the same set; the indices are retained in the definition of FzF_{z} below. For each z∈Xz\in X, define

Fz={y∈Y:Iy∈ℐ,z∈Iy}.F_{z}=\{y\in Y:I_{y}\in\mathcal{I},\ z\in I_{y}\}.

We claim that

|Fz|≤dG​(z)−2​r+3(z∈X).|F_{z}|\leq d_{G}(z)-2r+3\qquad(z\in X). (3.1)

If Fz=∅F_{z}=\varnothing, then |Fz|=0|F_{z}|=0. Since HH is α\alpha-critical without isolated vertices and α⁡(H)=r\alpha(H)=r, Lemma 2.2 gives dH​(z)≤n−2​r+1d_{H}(z)\leq n-2r+1. Since H=G¯H=\overline{G}, we obtain

dG​(z)=n−1−dH​(z)≥n−1−(n−2​r+1)=2​r−2.d_{G}(z)=n-1-d_{H}(z)\geq n-1-(n-2r+1)=2r-2.

Consequently,

|Fz|=0<1≤dG​(z)−2​r+3,|F_{z}|=0<1\leq d_{G}(z)-2r+3,

so (3.1) holds in this case.

Suppose Fz≠∅F_{z}\neq\varnothing. Let W=H⁡[V⁡(H)∖NH​[z]]W=H[V(H)\setminus N_{H}[z]] and let

D=⋃y∈Fz(Iy∖{z}),C=⋂y∈Fz(Iy∖{z}).D=\bigcup_{y\in F_{z}}(I_{y}\setminus\{z\}),\qquad C=\bigcap_{y\in F_{z}}(I_{y}\setminus\{z\}).

The sets {v}∪Iy\{v\}\cup I_{y}, for y∈Fzy\in F_{z}, are maximum independent sets of HH. Their union and intersection are {v,z}∪D\{v,z\}\cup D and {v,z}∪C\{v,z\}\cup C, respectively. Lemma 2.4 gives

|D|+|C|≥2​r−4.|D|+|C|\geq 2r-4. (3.2)

The sets {v}\{v\}, FzF_{z}, and DD are pairwise disjoint subsets of V⁡(W)V(W). Moreover, CC has no neighbors in any of them. Indeed, C⊆XC\subseteq X, so no vertex of CC is adjacent to vv; for every y∈Fzy\in F_{z}, we have C⊆IyC\subseteq I_{y}, so no vertex of CC is adjacent to yy; and if c∈Cc\in C and d∈Dd\in D, then d∈Iyd\in I_{y} for some y∈Fzy\in F_{z}, while c∈Iyc\in I_{y}, so c​d∉E⁡(H)cd\notin E(H). Thus NW​(C)N_{W}(C) is disjoint from all three sets. Since CC is an independent set of WW, Lemma 2.3 and (3.2) give

dG​(z)=|V​(W)|\displaystyle d_{G}(z)=|V(W)| ≥1+|Fz​|+|D|+|​NW​(C)|\displaystyle\geq 1+|F_{z}|+|D|+|N_{W}(C)| (3.3)
≥1+|Fz|+|D|+|C|\displaystyle\geq 1+|F_{z}|+|D|+|C|
≥|Fz|+2​r−3.\displaystyle\geq|F_{z}|+2r-3.

This proves (3.1) for every r≥2r\geq 2.

Finally, counting incidences between z∈Xz\in X and the chosen IyI_{y} gives ∑z∈X|Fz|=∑y∈Y|Iy|=(r−1)​|Y|\sum_{z\in X}|F_{z}|=\sum_{y\in Y}|I_{y}|=(r-1)|Y|. Summing (3.1) over XX therefore yields

∑z∈NG​(v)dG​(z)\displaystyle\sum_{z\in N_{G}(v)}d_{G}(z) ≥(2​r−3)​|X|+(r−1)​|Y|\displaystyle\geq(2r-3)|X|+(r-1)|Y|
=(r−2)​dG​(v)+(r−1)​(n−1),\displaystyle=(r-2)d_{G}(v)+(r-1)(n-1),

as required. ∎

For an integer r≥1r\geq 1, a graph GG, and v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), define the local surplus by

gr​(G,v)=∑w∈NG​(v)dG​(w)−(r−2)​dG​(v)−(r−1)​(|V⁡(G)|−r+1).g_{r}(G,v)=\sum_{w\in N_{G}(v)}d_{G}(w)-(r-2)d_{G}(v)-(r-1)(|V(G)|-r+1).

In the reduction below, deleting tt universal vertices preserves the surplus at every remaining vertex when the parameter is changed from rr to r−tr-t; see (3.4).If GG is Kr+1K_{r+1}-saturated with no universal vertex and r≥2r\geq 2, Proposition 3.1 gives gr​(G,v)≥(r−1)​(r−2)g_{r}(G,v)\geq(r-1)(r-2) for every v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G).

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

The graph GG is connected: every nonadjacent pair has a common (r−1)(r-1)-clique by saturation. Let AA be its adjacency matrix, ρ=ρ⁡(G)\rho=\rho(G), and q>0q>0 a Perron eigenvector. ≥0.\displaystyle\geq 0.

The quadratic has a negative root and a positive root, and thus ρ\rho is at least its positive root, as asserted.

Equality in the spectral bound forces gr​(G,v)=0g_{r}(G,v)=0 at every vertex, because all qvq_{v} are positive. Use tt, G0G_{0}, and k=r−tk=r-t from the preceding proof. If t>0t>0 and k≥2k\geq 2, (3.6) gives gr​(G,u)≥k⁡(k−1)>0g_{r}(G,u)\geq k(k-1)>0 at a universal vertex. Both alternatives are impossible, so k=1k=1. Consequently t=r−1t=r-1 and G0G_{0} is edgeless, yielding G≅Kr−1∨(n−r+1)​K1G\cong K_{r-1}\vee(n-r+1)K_{1}.

Conversely, let G=Kr−1∨(n−r+1)​K1G=K_{r-1}\vee(n-r+1)K_{1}, with clique part CC and independent-set part II. Every clique has order at most rr, while adding any missing edge u​vuv within II creates a Kr+1K_{r+1} on C∪{u,v}C\cup\{u,v\}. Thus GG is Kr+1K_{r+1}-saturated.

The partition (C,I)(C,I) is equitable, with quotient matrix

Q=(r−2n−r+1r−10).Q=\begin{pmatrix}r-2&n-r+1\\ r-1&0\end{pmatrix}.

Then (λ,r−1)𝖳(\lambda,r-1)^{\mathsf{T}} is a positive eigenvector of QQ. Proof of Corollary 1.5.

As in the proof of Theorem 1.3, GG is connected. Let AA be its adjacency matrix, ρ=ρ⁡(G)\rho=\rho(G), and q>0q>0 a Perron eigenvector. By (1.2), the vector

is entrywise nonnegative. Taking its inner product with qq and using the symmetry of AA, we obtain

(ρ2−(r−2)​ρ−(r−1)​(n−1))​∑vqv≥0.\bigl(\rho^{2}-(r-2)\rho-(r-1)(n-1)\bigr)\sum_{v}q_{v}\geq 0.

Taking the positive root gives (1.3). For G=C2​r+1¯G=\overline{C_{2r+1}}, we have n=2​r+1n=2r+1 and ρ⁡(G)=2​r−2\rho(G)=2r-2, and the right-hand side of (1.3) equals 2​r−22r-2. ∎

Remark 3.2.

The local inequality and the spectral lower bound also hold for r=2r=2, but the spectral equality graph is not unique: C5C_{5} already gives an additional example, since ρ⁡(C5)=2=5−1\rho(C_{5})=2=\sqrt{5-1}. This is why Theorem 1.3 assumes r≥3r\geq 3.
